title: Bagamoyo
subtitle: The caravan port was made a capital. Steamships could not dock there.
summary: The German East Africa Company made Bagamoyo the capital of the colony in January 1891, on the strength of its centuries-old standing as the coastal terminus of the interior caravan route. Its flat beach and poor anchorage were useless to steamships, and by early 1892 the administration had moved 75 kilometres south to the deep-water harbour at Dar es Salaam; the Boma built in 1895 to 1897 served out its life as a district office.
lesson: A location advantage expires with the transport technology that created it; audit why a place is valuable before you build a capital on the answer.
locationRole: Coastal town and short-lived colonial seat

title: African Minerals
subtitle: Sierra Leone's largest private employer could not survive one price cycle.
summary: African Minerals spent roughly $2.5 billion opening the Tonkolili iron ore mine, starting production in 2010 and forcibly relocating around 5,600 residents to clear the concession. Iron ore prices collapsed alongside the 2014 Ebola epidemic and in March 2015 the company suspended operations for lack of working capital, passing the asset to Shandong Iron and Steel and, after a licence revocation in 2019, to Kingho Mining.
lesson: A single-commodity balance sheet is a bet on the price curve, and the people moved off the land to place that bet do not get it back when it loses.
locationRole: Iron ore mine and rail concession

title: El Hamdania Port
subtitle: Nine years of drawings for one of Africa's largest ports. No quay was ever dug.
summary: Algeria signed with two Chinese state contractors in January 2016 to build its first deep-water port at Cherchell, specified for 23 quays and 6.5 million container units a year. Construction never began, the scheme was suspended during the Hirak protests of February 2019 and formally shelved by March 2025, leaving completed designs and impact assessments and no physical asset at all.
lesson: Signing a construction contract is not the same as holding the institutional capacity to manage one.
locationRole: Planned deep-water port site

title: Plan Obus
subtitle: A motorway with flats stacked inside it, aimed straight at the Casbah.
summary: From 1930 Le Corbusier spent four years proposing a restructuring of Algiers around a fourteen-level elevated roadtown housing some 180,000 people, with a business district at Cape of Algiers and a residential zone in the heights above the Casbah. Municipal authorities rejected it by unanimous vote in June 1942 and not one element of the scheme was ever built.
lesson: A plan that treats the existing city as an obstacle will be refused by the people living in it, however good the drawings are.
locationRole: Central city and the heights above the Casbah

title: The Algiers Metro
subtitle: Sixty-four kilometres promised. Twenty-eight years later, one line opened.
summary: Algeria proposed a 64-kilometre three-line metro for Algiers in 1982 and began construction in 1990, but the 1986 oil price collapse and the civil war of 1991 to 2002 reduced progress to 3,500 metres of tunnel across the whole of 1988 to 1999. Line 1 finally opened on 1 November 2011, a single route of roughly 9.5 to 13.2 kilometres against the original three-line network.
lesson: A capital project financed from commodity revenue inherits the commodity's cycle; phase it so a price crash costs you a phase rather than a decade.
locationRole: Metro alignment under the capital

title: Omo-Kuraz Sugar
subtitle: Two national parks were cut open for cane. One mill never got past a fifth.
summary: Ethiopia launched a six-factory sugar scheme in 2011 across 150,000 to 245,000 hectares of the Lower Omo Valley, on land excised from Omo and Mago national parks and irrigated from the Gibe III dam, without publishing the environmental and social assessments its own law required. By August 2022 Component VI stood about 20% complete and was excluded from privatisation for contractor underperformance, while the Sugar Corporation carried 11.3 billion birr of debt and displaced communities went uncompensated.
lesson: Skipping the assessment does not remove the constraint it would have found; it only defers the bill and removes your warning.
locationRole: Irrigated sugar blocks and mill sites

title: The Gwanda Solar Project
subtitle: A hundred megawatts contracted. One panel installed, for the security light.
summary: Zimbabwe Power Company awarded Intratrek a $172.8 million contract in October 2015 for a 100 megawatt solar plant on 262 hectares near Gwanda, and roughly $5.7 million was drawn before ZPC terminated the deal in April 2018 over unmet conditions precedent. The Supreme Court reinstated the contract in December 2023, but parliamentary inspectors in 2024 found the site overgrown, the buildings termite-eaten and a single panel running perimeter lighting.
lesson: Conditions precedent you do not control will strand you; secure the grid connection before you sign for the generation.
locationRole: Solar plant site

title: Nova Lisboa
subtitle: Renamed for a capital it never became, then almost erased by a civil war.
summary: Portuguese planners designated Huambo, in Angola's central highlands 600 kilometres from Luanda, as a modern colonial capital and formally renamed it Nova Lisboa in 1928. Luanda kept the seat of government, basic electricity, water and road connections did not arrive until the 1940s and 1950s, and the city was nearly obliterated in the post-independence war before recovering to become Angola's third largest at around 710,000 people.
lesson: Renaming a place does not relocate the institutions that make a capital function; declare the intent and the government still stays where its network is.
locationRole: Planned colonial capital

title: Konza Technopolis
subtitle: Kenya's Silicon Savannah. Google got tired of waiting and went to Kigali.
summary: Approved in 2008 under Vision 2030, Konza was to put a 5,000-acre smart city 60 kilometres from Nairobi and generate 100,000 jobs and $1 billion of annual revenue by 2020. Land acquisition rules introduced in 2012 stretched approvals from months to years, an anchor European university withdrew and Google redirected to Rwanda; Phase 1 infrastructure launched only in October 2025, with 16 operational tenants.
lesson: Approval speed is part of the product; when your clock runs in years the anchor tenant goes to whoever runs one in months.
locationRole: Technology city site on the Nairobi-Mombasa highway

title: The Lagos Metropolitan Rail
subtitle: Flagged off with a ceremony. Cancelled eighteen months later, nothing built.
summary: Governor Lateef Jakande launched a 28.5-kilometre elevated line from Marina to Agege in July 1983, contracted at N689 million to a nineteen-firm French consortium and designed for 88,000 passengers an hour across 19 stations. Buhari's incoming military government terminated it in January 1985, writing off about $78 million with no piling, corridor or rolling stock to show, and Lagos waited until September 2023 for its first light rail line.
lesson: A project owned by one administration is a liability the next one can cash in; anchor it in something harder than political patronage.
locationRole: Planned rail corridor from Marina to Agege

title: The Old Federal Secretariat
subtitle: Fifteen storeys on the most expensive land in Lagos, and nobody inside it.
summary: Built in 1976 across roughly 120,000 square metres of Ikoyi, the Secretariat housed Nigeria's federal civil service until the capital moved to Abuja in December 1991 and it emptied overnight. A 2006 concession to convert it into 480 flats collapsed when Lagos State refused residential zoning, and the building still stands derelict with foregone rent estimated at about N93.5 billion.
lesson: Decide the second use of a public asset before its first use ends; a building nobody owns the decision on simply rots where it stands.
locationRole: Federal office complex

title: The Lamu Coal Plant
subtitle: East Africa's biggest coal bet, beaten on a public participation argument.
summary: Amu Power was licensed in September 2016 to build a 1,050 megawatt coal-fired plant at Kwasaki, 20 kilometres from Lamu Town, at a cost of about $2 billion. Kenya's National Environmental Tribunal set the licence aside in June 2019 on procedural and constitutional grounds, General Electric and ICBC withdrew, and no construction ever began while 2,000 to 3,000 farmers were left holding land they cannot cultivate.
lesson: Consultation treated as a formality becomes the cheapest place for an opponent to beat you, and the one you cannot buy your way out of.
locationRole: Coal plant site on the Lamu coast

title: Kiwayu Safari Village
subtitle: Eighteen cottages, one night in September, and the whole coast emptied.
summary: Kiwayu Safari Village ran 18 thatched cottages on an island north of Lamu at $450 a person a night, employing about 120 permanent and seasonal staff. On 11 September 2011 gunmen killed the British visitor David Tebbutt and abducted his wife into Somalia; the resort closed within days, travel advisories pushed the exclusion zone out to 150 kilometres, and it never reopened.
lesson: A destination business cannot price its own risk alone; one incident on the coastline reprices every bed along it.
locationRole: Beach resort in the Kiunga Marine Reserve

title: Dutch Mauritius
subtitle: The ebony ran out before the colony learned how to feed itself.
summary: The Dutch East India Company settled Mauritius in 1638 and built fortifications, harbour works, cattle ranches, sugar and tobacco plantings and ebony logging camps for a population that never exceeded 25 to 50 colonists. Cyclones repeatedly destroyed the crops and herds, the ebony forests were logged out, pirates provisioned themselves at will, and the VOC evacuated the island for good in 1710.
lesson: An extractive venture has no second act; when the resource is exhausted, everything built to serve it becomes unfundable at once.
locationRole: Settlement and harbour of the VOC colony

title: Thabametsi Power Station
subtitle: The first South African coal plant made to account for its own carbon.
summary: Thabametsi was a 630 megawatt dry-cooled coal independent power producer near Lephalale, authorised in March 2015 and named preferred bidder in October 2016 at 80 cents a kilowatt-hour. A 2017 ruling made climate impact a mandatory part of environmental authorisation; Nedbank, Standard Bank, FirstRand and Absa retreated, the PIC, IDC, KEPCO and Marubeni followed, and the project was cancelled on 30 November 2020 with its approval set aside by the High Court.
lesson: When the legal test for a project changes mid-development, the financiers leave before the permit does.
locationRole: Coal plant site in the Waterberg

title: The Fengyue glass plant
subtitle: Botswana's move beyond diamonds cost it a quarter of a billion dollars.
summary: The Botswana Development Corporation put 447.84 million pula into a glass manufacturing plant at Palapye between 2007 and 2014, intended as the industrial anchor of a diamond-dependent economy. Cost and schedule overruns stopped construction before meaningful production began, and liquidation recovered only 67.8 million pula, leaving an unrecovered public loss of roughly 380 million pula.
lesson: Diversification does not reduce risk if the unfamiliar venture is monitored less closely than the familiar one.
locationRole: Glass manufacturing plant

title: Phalatswe
subtitle: Khama III built a capital, then walked his people away from it over water.
summary: Khama III moved the Bamangwato capital to Phalatswe in 1889 and built a full administrative town there, including a London Missionary Society church of 410 tonnes of burnt brick seating a thousand worshippers, much of it financed personally and built by mephato labour. The springs of the Photophoto Valley could not supply the population, and in 1902 Khama relocated the capital and most of its inhabitants 60 kilometres south to Serowe.
lesson: Verify the constraint that money cannot relieve before you build on top of it; water supply does not respond to further investment.
locationRole: Abandoned capital of the Bamangwato

title: KARMOL Nacala
subtitle: The powership that was to light northern Mozambique sailed to Brazil instead.
summary: Karpowership and MOL announced a floating LNG regasification and generation vessel for Nacala Harbour in August 2019, rated at about 50 megawatts and designed to avoid any shore-based terminal or land acquisition. Procurement began in 2021, but in 2022 the purpose-built powership was redeployed to Brazil, no replacement was secured, and the project was shelved by 2024.
lesson: Mobile assets follow the margin; a project whose core equipment can sail away is only as committed as its own returns.
locationRole: Harbour berth for a floating power plant

title: New Gourna
subtitle: Mud brick that cooled itself, built for villagers who did not want to move.
summary: Hassan Fathy designed New Gourna on the west bank at Thebes between 1945 and 1947 and it was built from 1946 to 1954, using Nubian vaulting, domed roofs and passive cooling to rehouse a village that had lived partly off the Theban necropolis. The relocated residents never took to a settlement they had not chosen, and after 2011 the village fell into neglect, its passive cooling failing as the fabric decayed.
lesson: Solving the climate does not solve the consent; a community that did not choose the building will not maintain it.
locationRole: Purpose-built village on the Nile west bank

title: Forte Tower
subtitle: Sadat's new Manhattan produced one concrete shell and a bedding showroom.
summary: Begun in the Sadat era as the first piece of a planned cluster of Nile-side skyscrapers, Forte Tower was designed as a 166-metre cylindrical building of 450 hotel rooms on Gezira Island in Zamalek. The concrete shell was completed but never fitted out; after Sadat's assassination in 1981 the original investor lost standing with the new presidency, litigation followed, and the structure has stood unfinished for roughly thirty years.
lesson: A permission granted by a person expires with that person; get the approval into an institution that will outlive the patron.
locationRole: Unfinished hotel tower on Gezira Island

title: Sadat City
subtitle: Ministries were moved out to the desert, and then quietly moved back.
summary: Sadat founded a replacement capital 94 kilometres north-west of Cairo in 1978, planned across some 500 square kilometres for over a million residents, five industrial zones and a green belt, and moved government ministries there at a cost of 25 million pounds. Officials found the distance unworkable, and after Sadat's assassination in 1981 the relocated ministries were handed to the University of Menoufia while the city settled into life as an industrial town of about 180 enterprises.
lesson: Moving the buildings does not move the network; a capital is mostly the proximity of the people who run it.
locationRole: Planned replacement capital

title: The Toshka Project
subtitle: Water pumped hundreds of kilometres into sand to grow a second Nile valley.
summary: Launched in 1997, Toshka was to lift water from Lake Nasser through a 310-kilometre concrete canal and reclaim 550,000 feddans in Phase 1 and two million more in Phase 2, anchored on the $400 million Mubarak Pumping Station completed in March 2005. Salinity, waterlogging and evaporation losses of around a tenth of Lake Nasser's annual inflow wrecked the economics, private capital never arrived, and Phase 2 was formally abandoned in 2005 with about 54,000 feddans irrigated by 2012.
lesson: If your plan assumes private capital funds three quarters of it, test that assumption before you build the quarter only the state can pay for.
locationRole: Reclamation area, canal and pumping station

title: The Qattara Depression Project
subtitle: Flood a desert basin with the Mediterranean and let gravity do the rest.
summary: From 1927 engineers proposed cutting a canal or tunnel 55 to 80 kilometres from the Mediterranean into the Qattara Depression, 60 metres below sea level, to drive turbines and fill an inland sea, a scheme examined by the CIA in 1957, German firms in the 1970s and Egyptian engineers under Sadat. Egypt commissioned a fresh feasibility study in April 2023 and formally abandoned the project in May 2026 on grounds of cost, groundwater salinisation and ecological damage.
lesson: An idea that keeps returning is not necessarily unfinished business; sometimes every generation simply has to redo the arithmetic and reach the same answer.
locationRole: Proposed canal route and inland sea basin

title: The Ada Toilets
subtitle: A million dollars a constituency for sanitation. The walls stopped at lintel height.
summary: Ghana's Infrastructure for Poverty Eradication Programme awarded contracts in 2017 for ten-seater toilet blocks across seventeen Ada communities and a rebuilt Kasseh Market, worth at least GHC4 million. By April 2023 none were finished, most standing roofless at lintel level, and the shells had been taken over as charcoal stores, refuse tips and cannabis hideouts while Ada East recorded 2,729 diarrhoea cases between 2020 and 2022.
lesson: A fixed contract price with no revaluation clause hands the cancellation decision to the contractor; inflation kills projects nobody ever cancels.
locationRole: Market and sanitation sites in Ada West and East

title: The Accra SkyTrain
subtitle: A monorail signed in Johannesburg, with the first station due in nine months.
summary: Ghana signed a $2.6 billion concession in November 2019 with a South African consortium for a 194-kilometre elevated automated monorail on five lines, carrying 380,000 passengers a day, with construction to begin in January 2020 and the first station open by August 2020. Nothing was built, financial close never happened and the consortium withdrew, leaving $2 million spent on feasibility studies the Auditor-General found inconclusive.
lesson: A concession signed before feasibility is settled transfers no risk; it only converts an unfinished study into a headline.
locationRole: Planned monorail network across Greater Accra

title: The Libyan Railway Network
subtitle: Locomotives in a warehouse, eight hundred staff, three kilometres of track.
summary: Libya announced a 3,170-kilometre standard-gauge national railway in 1998 and by 2008 and 2009 had signed $4.24 billion of contracts with China Railway Construction Corporation, Russian Railways and Ansaldo STS, taking delivery of 17 General Electric locomotives stored at Khoms. The February 2011 uprising suspended everything with three kilometres of track laid and $3.55 billion unexecuted, and the railway board was still staffed and drawing a payroll in 2016 with no trains to run.
lesson: Buying the rolling stock before the alignment exists locks capital into assets that cannot be redeployed when the schedule slips.
locationRole: Locomotive store on the coastal line

title: The Busabala Flyover
subtitle: The contractor left unpaid. The half-built junction kept collecting casualties.
summary: The Busabala junction interchange on Kampala's southern approach to the Entebbe expressway was contracted to China State Construction Engineering Corporation, which stopped work and left the site over Sh43 billion of unpaid invoices, part of Sh1.351 trillion in national road arrears by August 2026. The structure stands unfinished with temporary pavements and no signage or barriers, and on 3 May 2025 Rajiv Ruparelia was killed when his car struck them.
lesson: An abandoned worksite is not a paused cost; it keeps billing you, in a currency the budget line does not record.
locationRole: Unfinished road interchange

title: The Greater Kampala Light Rail
subtitle: Three manifestos, one master plan, eighteen years, and no track anywhere.
summary: A light rail network linking central Kampala to Port Bell, Namanve, Kira, Wakiso and Mukono first entered Uganda's National Transport Master Plan for 2008 to 2023 and was promised again in the ruling party's 2016 and 2021 manifestos, at an estimated cost above $1 billion. Nothing was ever built; a Namanve to Kampala pilot service carried 942,982 passengers between 2015 and 2018 before being suspended, and in March 2026 the government signed an 18-month feasibility study with Orascom.
lesson: Repeating a commitment is far cheaper than funding one; treat a re-announcement without a budget line as evidence against delivery.
locationRole: Planned light rail network
